chapters.chapter_title: Lesson 14: Summarize spoken text and Highlight correct summary

estimated_study_time.text: Plan one focused study session of about 2 hours, plus extra time for homework practice if needed.

chapter_summary.text: This chapter provides skills practice for Summarize spoken text and Highlight correct summary. It focuses on listening, reading, and writing skills including identifying main ideas, summarizing, recognizing supporting points, understanding speaker purpose or attitude, following lecture sequence, taking notes while listening, writing summaries, and choosing the most accurate summary.

evidence_spans.quote:
This lesson provides skills practice for the PTE Academic item types Summarize spoken text and Highlight correct 
summary.

Listening
• Identifying the topic, theme or main ideas
• Summarizing the main idea
• Identifying supporting points or examples
• Identifying a speaker’s purpose, style, tone or attitude

• Following an oral sequencing of information
• Comprehending variations in tone, speed, accent
Reading
• Identifying supporting points or examples
• Identifying the most accurate summary

Writing
• Writing a summary 
• Writing under timed conditions
• Taking notes while listening to a recording
• Communicating the main points of a lecture in writing

meaning.text: Signpost words are signal words used by lecturers to show lecture structure, emphasize main ideas, and distinguish main ideas from supporting details.

evidence_spans.quote:
lecturers also use signal words to give their listeners ‘signposts’ of a lecture’s 
structure, to emphasize main ideas, and to distinguish main ideas from supporting details.

meaning.text: Redundant information is bracketed text: ideas that are inaccurate or ideas not mentioned by the speaker.

evidence_spans.quote:
Tell test takers to put ideas that are inaccurate in curly brackets { }, and ideas not mentioned 
by the speaker in square brackets [ ]. Explain that bracketed text is redundant information

meaning.text: Speaker attitude refers to whether the speaker has a strong, weak, or neutral opinion and whether the speaker views something favorably or unfavorably.

evidence_spans.quote:
whether the speaker has a strong, weak or neutral 
opinion about the topic, and whether the speaker regards something favorably or unfavorably

meaning.text: A summary is a brief statement that accurately represents the topic and main points of a written or spoken text.

evidence_spans.quote:
A summary is a brief 
statement that accurately represents the topic and main points of a written or spoken text.

explanation.text: The lesson covers Summarize spoken text and Highlight correct summary, including their format, rubrics, scoring, strategies, and timed practice.

evidence_spans.quote:
test takers will look at the Summarize spoken text and Highlight correct summary 
item types

they will look closely at the format, rubrics and scoring of these item types; analyze strategies 
for approaching them successfully, and complete practice items under timed conditions.

explanation.text: When listening, note key words rather than every word because the aim is to identify the topic and the most important information.

evidence_spans.quote:
The ‘listeners’ in each pair should only note key words, not every word, as the aim is to 
identify the topic and most important information.

core_lessons.title: Use Signpost Words To Follow Lectures

explanation.text: Signpost words help listeners understand lecture structure, order key points, identify the main topic, and notice emphasis.

evidence_spans.quote:
‘Today I’d like to…’ signals the lecturer’s main topic; ‘three main strategies’ signals the lecture’s 3-
part structure

Sequencing words and 
phrases such as ‘my first piece of advice’, ‘firstly’, ‘secondly’, and ‘last but not least’ help to order 
key points

words such as ‘always …’, ‘make sure to …’, ‘it is also very important 
to’ signal emphasis.

explanation.text: A speaker’s attitude or opinion can be inferred from vocabulary, including words that express positive, negative, neutral, certain, or uncertain attitudes.

evidence_spans.quote:
the attitude or opinion of a speaker can be inferred by looking at the vocabulary 
used

At the top of the first three columns write the following headings 
‘positive’, ‘negative’, ‘neutral’.
a lecturer can also display an attitude which is certain or uncertain.

explanation.text: A summary accurately represents the topic and main points, usually omits examples, often uses complex noun phrases and the simple present tense, and does not retell personal information or give a narrative.

evidence_spans.quote:
A summary is a brief 
statement that accurately represents the topic and main points of a written or spoken text. Examples 
are usually omitted.
they often contain complex noun phrases to describe the main ideas.

The simple present tense is often used because the writer is giving a factual statement of the main 
points. A summary does not retell personal information or give a narrative.

explanation.text: For Highlight correct summary, eliminate paragraphs with incorrect information, information not mentioned in the recording, or details that omit the main or important points.

evidence_spans.quote:
eliminate the 
paragraphs that obviously contain incorrect information. Then, eliminate the paragraphs that contain information 
that is not mentioned in the recording.

you should try 
to eliminate paragraphs which contain details but which omit the main or important points.

worked_examples.title: Note Only Key Words From A Mini Lecture

example.text: Listen to a short lecture about three study strategies. Write only key words such as topic, first strategy, second strategy, final strategy, and any repeated emphasis words. After listening, compare your notes with a partner and ask for spelling clarification on unclear key words.

explanation.text: This practice matches the lesson procedure: one learner reads a lecture aloud, the listener notes key words, and unclear vocabulary or spelling can be checked after speaking.

evidence_spans.quote:
‘A’s and ‘B’s should take turns reading out their lecture to their partner in a clear voice 
and at a slightly slower than normal speed
The ‘listeners’ in each pair should only note key words, not every word

they can ask the ‘lecturers’ for 
verification of vocabulary and correct spelling, and revise or correct their notes as necessary.

example.text: After listening to a lecture, read four possible summaries. Mark any statement that contradicts your notes as inaccurate. Mark any statement that your notes do not support as not mentioned. Eliminate those options and choose the remaining summary that best preserves the main ideas.

explanation.text: The lesson trains learners to identify main ideas in each summary, decide whether ideas are accurate, inaccurate, or not presented, eliminate summaries containing redundant information, and select the most accurate summary.

evidence_spans.quote:
before choosing a summary they should first identify the main ideas in each one 
and determine whether these ideas are accurate, inaccurate or not presented in the lecture.
summaries containing any bracketed information can be eliminated.

Once test takers have eliminated those summaries containing redundant information, tell them to 
select the most accurate summary

misconception.text: In a listening task, the best notes are word-for-word notes of everything the speaker says.

correction.text: Listeners should note key words, not every word, because the aim is to identify the topic and most important information.

evidence_spans.quote:
The ‘listeners’ in each pair should only note key words, not every word, as the aim is to 
identify the topic and most important information.

misconception.text: For Highlight correct summary, it is best to read the answer options before listening to the recording.

correction.text: For this item type, learners should focus first on listening and note-taking, then look at the options; looking at the options first may distract them.

evidence_spans.quote:
for this item type it is very important to first remain focused on listening to 
the recording and taking notes and to look at the options after that.

Looking at the options before they 
complete the listening and note-taking part of the item may distract them from what they hear.

misconception.text: A summary should retell the lecture as a personal story or narrative.

correction.text: A summary is a brief statement of the topic and main points; it does not retell personal information or give a narrative.

evidence_spans.quote:
A summary is a brief 
statement that accurately represents the topic and main points of a written or spoken text.
A summary does not retell personal information or give a narrative.

question.text: You hear a lecture that begins, “Today I’d like to talk about three major reasons for urban migration. First... Now let’s move on... Finally...” What should you listen for and note?

answer.text: Note the main topic, the three sequenced main points, and key words connected to each point. Do not try to write every word.

question.text: After listening to a lecture, one summary contains a correct detail but leaves out the main point. Should that option remain a strong candidate?

answer.text: No. Eliminate summaries that contain details but omit the main or important points.

question.text: A speaker says, “Without doubt, this is a major problem,” and later says, “perhaps this may improve.” Which words help you judge certainty or uncertainty?

answer.text: “Without doubt” and “major problem” suggest certainty, while “perhaps” and “may” suggest uncertainty.

question.text: When checking a written summary of a spoken text, what should you check before finalizing it?

answer.text: Check whether it contains all key information, has the required word count, and uses correct grammar, spelling, and punctuation.

review_checklist.text: I can identify a lecture’s topic and main ideas from signpost words and stressed key words.
I can take notes using key words instead of trying to write every word.
I can use vocabulary clues to infer whether a speaker’s opinion is positive, negative, neutral, certain, or uncertain.
I can eliminate summaries that contain inaccurate information, information not mentioned in the lecture, or details that miss the main point.
I can write a concise summary that states the topic and main points without turning the lecture into a narrative.
